activities.caption: call the gas volume the syringe will hold
activities.name: kinMgEst

config.prompt: 0.12 g of magnesium (0.005 mol) in excess acid releases 0.005 mol of hydrogen. Roughly what volume does that occupy at room temperature?
config.why: About 120 cm³ — the early average runs 1.5 cm³/s while the rest crawls over 5 minutes: fewer effective collisions as the acid is consumed.
config.context: Molar gas volume ≈ 24,000 cm³ per mol — 0.005 mol × 24,000 = 120 cm³.

activities.caption: file each move by which dial it turns
activities.name: kinDialSort

config.prompt: Every rate factor is a dial on one statement — file each move by what it changes:
buckets: clear the energy bar more easily

items.label: double the acid concentration — magnesium fizzes about twice as fast
swap a chalk chip for powder — ten thousandfold more reactive frontier
double the pressure of a gas reaction
raise the temperature — the fast tail of the energy distribution grows
add iron to the ammonia bed — a lower-energy route

config.why: Enough energy and the right orientation: turn any dial and one of those two improves.

activities.anchor: only makes particles move faster, so collisions
activities.caption: find the faulty line — why heat is so violent a lever
activities.name: kinHeatSpot

config.prompt: A student explains the 10 °C doubling rule. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: Warming lifts the collision frequency a little — by about √T.
The violence of the effect comes from the energy distribution's tail.
A 10 °C rise roughly doubles the fraction of molecules carrying enough energy to react.
The modest speed increase is what runs the world.
Cold kills difficult reactions first — which is exactly why refrigeration preserves food.
config.correction: It is the exponential statistics, not the speedometer, that runs the world — Arrhenius: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT).
config.why: Frequency climbs modestly; the fraction clearing Ea roughly doubles per 10 °C — the exponential does the work.

activities.caption: which curve is the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution?
activities.name: kinMBTrace

config.prompt: Molecular energy against fraction of molecules — which curve, shaded past the bar, is the fraction that can react?
config.why: The long-tailed curve: heating stretches the tail — exponentially more area past the bar; a catalyst drags the bar leftward into the bulk; concentration just rescales the whole picture.

activities.anchor: leaded petrol famously gummed converter surfaces
activities.caption: true or false — what a catalyst never does
activities.name: kinCatJudge

statements.s: A catalyst is consumed as it works and must be continually replaced.
statements.why: It participates and is regenerated — a converter's platinum survives a decade of exhausts.

statements.s: A catalyst lowers the activation hill for the forward and reverse paths alike.
statements.why: Same lower road both ways — so it buys time, never yield.

statements.s: No catalyst in history has shifted an equilibrium position.
statements.why: It accelerates both directions equally; position and K are untouched, however much industry wished otherwise.

statements.s: Enzymes accelerate reactions by factors of 10⁶ to beyond 10¹⁷.
statements.why: Carbonic anhydrase hydrates about a million CO₂ molecules per second per enzyme.

activities.anchor: is where chemistry and medicine meet
activities.caption: walk the clock on a 6-hour half-life
activities.name: kinHalfBranch

config.root: One dose at noon; the label promises a 6-hour first-order half-life. Walk the clock.

start.text: Noon — 100% of the dose in the blood. What is true by 18:00?

choices.label: One half-life has passed — 50% remains
choices.feedback: 6 hours → 50%. First order: the same fraction falls each half-life.

choices.label: It depends on how big the dose was
choices.feedback: For first-order decay the fraction is fixed — large dose or small, half is gone every 6 hours.

dose.text: First-order decay halves the PERCENTAGE each half-life: 50, 25, 12.5… the amount depends on the dose, the fraction never does.

evening.text: 18:00 — 50% remains. Midnight is two half-lives in. What is left by 06:00?

choices.label: 0% — the last of it clears at midnight
choices.feedback: First order never reaches zero: 12.5% at three half-lives, 6.25% at four — the tail thins forever.

morning.text: By 06:00 five half-lives have passed: about 3% remains — the mathematics behind carbon-14 dating, clearance curves and every exponential decay.

zero.text: Zero never arrives: each 6-hour tick halves what is left — 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25…

config.why: First-order decay carries a constant half-life — the mathematics behind carbon-14 dating, clearance curves and every exponential decay.
